summaries.example: Imagine two backpacks. Your old backpack has strong zippers, wide straps, and a padded back. A new backpack has the same features. You guess that the new backpack may also be comfortable. This is an analogy: you use known similarities to suggest another similarity. The guess is reasonable, but it could still be wrong if the new backpack has a hidden problem.
summaries.summary: An analogy compares two things or systems because they seem alike in some ways. Analogical reasoning uses that comparison to suggest something further. For example, if two medicines have similar features and one works in a certain way, researchers may investigate whether the other works similarly. The comparison may help discover an idea, explain a problem, or support a guess. But an analogy does not normally make its conclusion certain. Its strength depends on which similarities and differences are present and whether they are relevant. Philosophers have proposed many ways to judge analogies, such as looking for important relationships, causes, or patterns. They disagree about whether one general rule can cover all cases. The entry explains that analogies are useful tools, but they need careful checking.
key_ideas: Analogies help people notice ideas, solve problems, and suggest new questions.
An analogical argument uses similarities between a source and a target to support a further claim about the target.
An analogy can be strong, weak, or misleading. Similarities must be relevant to the conclusion.
An analogy usually gives support, not a guarantee. More testing or evidence may be needed.
There is no single simple rule that tells us when every analogy is good.
Analogies can guide science and other kinds of thinking, but they can also lead people in the wrong direction.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use comparisons every day, in school, science, law, and ordinary decisions. Learning about analogy helps us ask whether a comparison truly supports a conclusion or only sounds convincing. It also shows how new ideas can begin: an analogy may point researchers toward a question worth investigating. At the same time, noticing differences protects us from trusting a comparison too quickly.

important_terms.definition: A comparison between two things that points out ways they are alike.
Thinking from known similarities to a possible new similarity.
The thing or situation we already know about and use for comparison.
The thing or situation we are trying to understand or predict.
A claim that has some support and is worth taking seriously, but is not certain.

questions_to_think_about: Which similarities between two things really matter for the guess being made?
Can a comparison have many similarities and still be a bad analogy?
What difference between two things might make an analogy misleading?
When should an analogy lead us to test an idea instead of believing it?

summaries.example: Suppose a researcher studies a drug whose chemical structure resembles that of a familiar pain medicine. An effect observed with the familiar drug may make a similar effect in the new drug plausible, encouraging further tests. The analogy does not establish the effect by itself: the two drugs may differ in properties that matter, and researchers may not yet know all the relevant factors. The comparison is therefore a reason for investigation, not a substitute for evidence.
summaries.summary: The entry studies analogical arguments as a central but contested form of reasoning. In the basic pattern, a source and a target agree in some accepted respects; the source has an additional feature; and the argument proposes that the target has that feature, or an appropriate counterpart. The conclusion is normally ampliative rather than deductively guaranteed. It may express a degree of probability, or it may establish only prima facie plausibility—the status of being worth serious investigation. Philosophers have proposed common-sense, causal, material, structural, computational, practice-based, and articulation-based approaches to evaluation. These approaches disagree because overall similarity is not enough: similarities can be irrelevant, differences can matter differently, and the importance of a feature depends on the particular inquiry. The entry also examines attempts to justify analogy through deduction, induction, a priori principles, or practical values. None supplies an uncontroversial universal logic of analogy. Analogies nevertheless remain important in scientific discovery, legal reasoning, model-building, and the development of new theories. Their usefulness depends on critical examination and on combining them with other forms of reasoning and evidence.
key_ideas: A standard analogical argument begins with known similarities between source and target, adds a feature of the source, and projects a corresponding feature onto the target.
Analogical conclusions are generally ampliative: they may be supported without being certain. Plausibility can be understood probabilistically or as a preliminary reason to investigate a claim.
Simple guidelines—more similarities, fewer differences, causal connections, structural correspondences, and relevant evidence—are useful but can conflict or remain too vague.
A formal pattern alone cannot distinguish good analogies from bad ones. An analogy can contain many similarities that have nothing to do with its conclusion.
Different approaches emphasize different factors: material and causal relations, formal structure, goals and context, local facts, or practices within a particular field.
Analogies serve both discovery and justification. They may guide a research program or help develop concepts, yet a guiding analogy can eventually fail or mislead.
summaries.why_it_matters: Analogical reasoning connects creativity with criticism. It can generate hypotheses when direct observation or a complete theory is unavailable, and it can organize inquiry by suggesting that two systems share a deeper pattern. But its flexibility creates a danger: a formally neat or rhetorically vivid comparison may support nothing if its similarities are irrelevant. Studying analogy therefore clarifies how scientific, mathematical, legal, and everyday arguments move from what is known toward what is not yet established.

important_terms.definition: A comparison between objects or systems that identifies selected correspondences between them.
Reasoning that uses an analogy to reach a further claim, prediction, or hypothesis.
The domain from which known features or relations are taken in an analogical argument.
The domain to which a further feature or relation is projected.
The known similarities used in an argument; known differences are sometimes called negative analogy.
A conclusion supported to some degree but not entailed by the premises. It may mean probable in degree or worthy of initial investigation.
Reasoning whose conclusion extends beyond what is guaranteed by its premises.
A proposed general pattern that would make a conclusion follow deductively from information about the source and target.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a weak conclusion be better supported by analogy than a strong conclusion?
Should structural similarity matter more than visible similarity? What would depend on the subject?
Why does adding similarities not always strengthen an analogical argument?
Can a deductive rule fully justify an analogy, or would the difficult work move into defending the rule?
How might an analogy guide research even if it eventually turns out to be false?

summaries.example: A student notices that two study apps both use short quizzes, reminders, and progress charts. The first app helped her remember vocabulary, so she predicts that the second may also help with science terms. This is a reasonable analogical argument, but it is not a sure thing. The second app might have confusing questions or a different way of giving feedback. The similarities matter only if they are connected to remembering.
summaries.summary: An analogy compares two objects, cases, or systems in selected respects. Analogical reasoning uses that comparison to suggest that a further feature of the source may also belong to the target. An argument by analogy therefore has a source, a target, known similarities, and a proposed similarity. Its conclusion is usually not certain. Instead, it receives some degree of support or becomes plausible enough to deserve investigation. Philosophers have suggested several evaluation guidelines: more relevant similarities can help, important differences can hurt, causal or structural connections may matter, and several independent comparisons may add support. Yet these guidelines are not a complete rulebook. A comparison can have many similarities that are irrelevant, while a single difference may be decisive. Some theories focus on formal patterns between systems; others stress observable features, causal relations, practical purposes, or facts specific to the field. The entry also explains that analogy is used not only to defend conclusions but to discover ideas and develop theories. Because analogies can both illuminate and mislead, they should be tested and considered alongside other evidence.
key_ideas: Analogical arguments move from known similarities to a proposed similarity that has not yet been established.
The conclusion is usually supported rather than guaranteed, so analogy differs from strict deduction.
Relevant similarities matter more than simply having a large number of similarities. Causal or structural connections may be especially important in some cases.
Philosophers disagree about how analogy works: some emphasize overall similarity, some formal structure, some causes, and some the local facts and purposes of a particular case.
A simple rule for analogical inference would allow too many bad arguments, because unrelated similarities can be counted as support.
Analogy can help discover hypotheses, justify limited claims, guide research, and shape new concepts. It can also create misleading expectations.
summaries.why_it_matters: Analogies influence how people explain unfamiliar ideas and decide what to try next. Scientists may use them to form hypotheses, lawyers may compare a new case with an earlier one, and students may use a familiar problem to understand a new topic. Knowing how analogical reasoning works helps us appreciate its creative power while asking whether the comparison is relevant, whether important differences have been ignored, and whether the conclusion is stronger than the support allows.

important_terms.definition: A comparison that highlights selected ways in which two things or systems are alike.
Using similarities between a known case and a new case to support a further claim about the new case.
The known case used as the basis for a comparison.
The case about which a new claim is being made.
The similarities accepted before the new conclusion is drawn.
A difference between the source and target that may weaken the comparison.
Support that makes a claim worth considering without proving it.

questions_to_think_about: What makes a similarity relevant instead of merely noticeable?
How could a known difference change the strength of an analogy?
Why might two people disagree about whether the same analogy is convincing?
Is an analogy more useful for making a prediction or for suggesting a question to investigate?
Can a comparison guide research even when it does not prove the final idea?
